Being a spotter

Watch the sky. Say it short. When in doubt, call "Land!".

▶  Present the slides

Sooner or later someone hands you this job: "Can you spot for me?" Often it's a parent at the edge of a field, with a kid in goggles and no idea what to do. Good news: you don't need to know anything about drones. You need good eyes, a few short words, and the courage to say "Land!".

In goggles, the pilot is blind

A pilot in FPV goggles sees only what the drone's camera sees: one small window, pointing wherever the drone points. Everything around the drone, the plane coming in low, the walker with a dog, the kid running onto the field, is outside that window. That's the spotter's job.

Outdoors it's also the law. When you fly with goggles on, the pilot isn't looking at the drone, and the rules only allow that if an observer stands right next to the pilot, keeps their own eyes on the drone and the sky, and warns the pilot straight away. It's not a formality: low planes and helicopters do fly over the fields where we fly, and a pilot in goggles never sees them coming. (For the full rules, see the talk "Where am I allowed to fly?".)

Who can spot?

Anyone who can see well and stays focused. At races, every second pilot spots for someone else, and then they swap. A team-mate from the club who isn't flying right now makes a good spotter too. But most often it's mum or dad, and usually with no warning: you came to drive, and suddenly you're part of the flight. This guide is mostly for you.

Stand right next to the pilot

Stand next to the pilot, not behind them, close enough to touch their shoulder, so a warning reaches them at once. Face the same way they do: that way you see the pilot, the drone and the sky at once.

Use your own eyes. No goggles, no phone screen, no binoculars. If you can't see the drone with your own eyes, it's too far away. And give one pilot all of your attention: don't chat, don't film, don't wander off to get a coffee. If you have to leave, the pilot lands first.

What to watch, in this order

The drone is the pilot's problem. The world around it is yours. Watch in this order:

1. The sky. Planes, helicopters, other drones. Listen too: you often hear a helicopter long before you see it. 2. People and animals. Walkers, kids, dogs and cars heading towards the flying area. 3. The drone. Where is it? Can you still see it? Did it go down, and where?

Say it short, the same way every time

When something happens, there's no time for sentences. Agree the words before the flight, and say them loudly:

  • "Heli!" or "Plane!": something in the sky.
  • "People!": someone is coming onto the field.
  • "Land!": the pilot lands now, right where the drone is.
  • "Lost it!": you can't see the drone any more.
  • "Down!": it crashed, and you're watching where.

The pilot answers "OK!" or "Landing!", so you know the message got through. No answer? Say it again, louder. Still nothing? Tap their shoulder.

Add a landmark when it helps: "Heli, over the big tree!" tells the pilot where to look out. Landmarks help the pilot too. In goggles even experienced pilots lose their bearings, and "Fly towards the big tree" brings them back.

When to say "Land!"

Say it when something in the sky is coming your way, low. When someone walks into the flying area or is heading there. When you lose sight of the drone behind trees, or it's too far or too high. And when something just feels wrong: the drone wobbles, the pilot sounds unsure, the wind picks up.

You never have to explain why. "Land!" means land, and you can talk about it afterwards.

The drone doesn't matter. However expensive it is, you're not there to protect the drone. You're there so the flight is safe, and that safety is for everything else: the people, the animals, the other aircraft in the sky. Drones break, crash and get lost, and that's part of the hobby. A drone that lands in the wrong place or crashes because you called "Land!" too early is a good trade. The pilot may disagree, especially in the middle of a good flight. That's fine: the pilot lands first, and you argue later.

What a spotter never does

A spotter helps, but the pilot is still the pilot, and the flight is their responsibility. So:

  • Never grab the radio, even if it goes wrong. Say "Land!" and let the pilot do it.
  • Never look at a screen. No phone, no filming, not even "just a second".
  • No binoculars. The rule is your own eyes. If you need binoculars to see the drone, it's too far.

Spotting at a race

At a race the spotter can be another pilot, a team-mate, or mum or dad. The job is the same, with a few extra rules. Stay in the pilot area next to your pilot and never walk onto the track while anyone is flying. Listen to the race director: their calls come first, before anything you or your pilot want. And if your pilot crashes, remember where the drone came down, tell the pilot and the marshal, and pick it up only when the heat is over.

Mum or dad: five minutes before you start

Most spotters are parents, and nobody told them what to do. So before the first battery, take five minutes with your pilot and agree:

1. Where exactly? Where the flying area ends, and what's off limits. 2. Which words? Practise the calls out loud: Heli! People! Land! Lost it! Down! 3. Which landmarks? Pick a few that you both can see: the big tree, the gate, the shed. Then a call can say where: "Heli, over the big tree!" or "It went down left of the gate." 4. What if it crashes? You watch where it falls. Nobody runs out while others are flying. 5. When do we land? Ask how long a flight lasts, and agree when to come down. 6. Who's in charge? The pilot flies, you watch. Your "Land!" is always obeyed.

Do I need a licence? Usually not: a spotter doesn't need a certificate. But if your pilot is under 16, you're not just the spotter, you're the qualified adult supervising them, and then you need the A1/A3 certificate yourself. Don't worry. It's an online test at Transpordiamet's LOIS portal, 40 questions, and one of the easiest tests you'll ever take. (More in the talk "Where am I allowed to fly?".)

After a crash, you're also the best search party: you saw where it went down. And if you want to know more, ask the trainer at the club. Many parents end up flying too.

Watch the sky. Say it short. When in doubt, call "Land!".

Demo: Pair up: one "pilot" with eyes closed holding an imaginary radio, one spotter next to them. The trainer walks around the room as a "helicopter", a "walker" or a "dog". The spotter calls it, the pilot answers. Then swap. Parents first.
